topic.body: A plain abdominal radiograph and excretory urography are different examinations. Urography uses contrast to depict the urinary tract; a plain film does not provide that opacification.
bullets: Distinguish the renal outline from the collecting system and ureter.
No excretion, obstruction or renal function can be inferred from this intact reference surface.

topic.body: On a plain abdominal radiograph, orient the renal regions beside the lumbar spine and any visible psoas margins. Renal soft-tissue outlines may be only partly discernible; their visibility depends on surrounding fat contrast and overlapping abdominal contents. A visible outer shadow is not a view of the internal collecting system.
bullets: Confirm the recorded patient side, projection and image coverage before comparing the two renal regions. A poorly seen outline does not establish an absent or abnormal kidney.
A projected opacity is not automatically a urinary calculus. Stone radiopacity varies with composition; some stones are radiolucent, so a negative plain film cannot exclude them.
Intravenous pyelography uses injected iodinated contrast and timed radiographs to outline the urinary tract. It is a different examination from a non-contrast plain film or CT/MR urography.

Reassemble the atlas before studying spatial relationships. This outer surface supplies no radiographic attenuation, collecting-system opacification, stone diagnosis, excretion, obstruction assessment or renal function.
